```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_igraph <- requireNamespace("igraph", quietly = TRUE)
has_network <- requireNamespace("network", quietly = TRUE)
```

knappnet works on networks stored as two data frames, one for nodes and one
for edges. Every measure returns a vector (or a data frame) aligned with the
rows of the node table, so results become ordinary columns that you can
summarize, plot, or model with the tools you already use.

This vignette covers the essentials: building a network, computing
measures, weights, conversion to and from other packages, and files. If
you already use another tool, the guides on the website map its functions
to knappnet's:
[igraph](https://knapply.github.io/knappnet/articles/coming-from-igraph.html),
[statnet and sna](https://knapply.github.io/knappnet/articles/coming-from-statnet.html),
[UCINET, ORA, Pajek, and Gephi](https://knapply.github.io/knappnet/articles/coming-from-ucinet-ora-pajek-gephi.html),
and [NetworkX](https://knapply.github.io/knappnet/articles/coming-from-networkx.html).

```{r}
library(knappnet)
```

## Networks are two data frames

Padgett's data on marriages among leading families of Renaissance Florence
(Breiger and Pattison 1986) is a classic first network. Each row of `ties`
is a marriage tie between two families:

```{r}
ties <- data.frame(
  from = c("Acciaiuoli", "Medici", "Medici", "Medici", "Medici", "Medici",
           "Castellani", "Castellani", "Castellani", "Peruzzi", "Peruzzi",
           "Strozzi", "Strozzi", "Ridolfi", "Tornabuoni", "Albizzi", "Albizzi",
           "Salviati", "Bischeri", "Guadagni"),
  to   = c("Medici", "Barbadori", "Ridolfi", "Tornabuoni", "Albizzi", "Salviati",
           "Peruzzi", "Strozzi", "Barbadori", "Strozzi", "Bischeri",
           "Ridolfi", "Bischeri", "Tornabuoni", "Guadagni", "Ginori", "Guadagni",
           "Pazzi", "Guadagni", "Lamberteschi")
)
```

The Pucci family married outside this group, so it appears in no tie. A
node table keeps it in the network as an isolate, and holds any node
attributes:

```{r}
families <- data.frame(name = sort(unique(c(ties$from, ties$to, "Pucci"))))
flo <- netframe(ties, nodes = families, directed = FALSE)
flo
```

Without `nodes`, the node table is built from the edge list, in order of
first appearance, and isolates are necessarily missing. `netframe()`
assumes the endpoints are the first two columns of the edge table and the
identifier is the first column of the node table; `from`, `to`, and `id`
name other columns. Any other columns are attributes and are carried
along untouched.

The two tables are plain data frames:

```{r}
head(flo$nodes)
head(flo$edges)
```

## Measures

Each node-level measure returns one value per row of `flo$nodes`, in the
same order, so results can be stored directly as columns:

```{r}
flo$nodes$degree <- degree(flo)
flo$nodes$betweenness <- betweenness(flo)
flo$nodes$harmonic <- round(harmonic_centrality(flo, normalized = TRUE), 3)
flo$nodes$core <- coreness(flo)
flo$nodes[order(-flo$nodes$betweenness), ]
```

The Medici lie on far more shortest paths between other families than
anyone else, in line with Padgett and Ansell's (1993) account of the
family's rise, which stresses its ties to families that were not tied to
one another.

Harmonic centrality is shown here instead of closeness because the Pucci
cannot reach anyone. Closeness sums distances to the other nodes, and
programs disagree about what to do with distances that do not exist:

```{r}
closeness(flo)[flo$nodes$name == "Pucci"]
```

Under igraph's convention, the default, a node that reaches no one gets
`NaN`. The `convention` argument reproduces the choices of NetworkX, sna,
or UCINET instead; `?conventions` and the
[conventions guide](https://knapply.github.io/knappnet/articles/conventions.html)
explain every difference.

Measures of the whole network return a single number, or a list:

```{r}
graph_density(flo)
centralization(flo, "degree")
comp <- components(flo)
comp$no
comp$csize
```

Groups of nodes are returned as membership vectors aligned with the nodes,
or as lists of node identifiers:

```{r}
max_cliques(flo, min_size = 3)
groups <- cluster_louvain(flo, seed = 1)
table(groups)
```

Louvain community detection visits nodes in a random order, so it takes a
seed; the same seed gives the same result on any computer and with any
number of threads. Without one, a seed is drawn from R's generator, so
`set.seed()` works as usual.

## Weighted networks

A network without a weight column is binary, and every algorithm uses its
fastest unweighted form. With weights, you say once what they mean.
Distances (travel time, cost, latency) keep nodes apart:

```{r}
roads <- data.frame(
  from    = c("a", "b", "a"),
  to      = c("b", "c", "c"),
  minutes = c(5, 5, 20)
)
trips <- netframe(roads, directed = FALSE, weight = "minutes")
trips
betweenness(trips)                    # a to c is quicker through b
betweenness(trips, weighted = FALSE)  # ignoring travel time
```

Strengths (contact frequency, tie intensity) bring nodes closer, so
path-based measures use 1/weight as the length, while measures that add up
weights use them as given:

```{r}
calls <- data.frame(
  from  = c("a", "b", "a"),
  to    = c("b", "c", "c"),
  calls = c(1, 1, 20)
)
phone <- netframe(calls, directed = FALSE, weight = "calls", weight_type = "strength")
betweenness(phone)  # a and c talk directly, so b brokers nothing
strength(phone)
```

Path-based measures take `weighted` (use the weights or not) and
`weights_as` (read them as `"distance"` or `"strength"` for this call
only). Measures defined only on binary ties, such as cliques, the triad
census, and brokerage, ignore weights and say so in their help pages.

## Conversion

`as.matrix()` gives the adjacency matrix, and `as_netframe()` turns a
matrix back into a network. Direction is inferred from symmetry, and
values other than 0 and 1 become weights:

```{r}
m <- matrix(c(0, 2, 0,
              2, 0, 1,
              0, 1, 0), 3, byrow = TRUE,
            dimnames = list(c("x", "y", "z"), c("x", "y", "z")))
small <- as_netframe(m)
small
small$edges
as.matrix(small, attr = "weight")
```

Networks also convert both ways with igraph, tidygraph, and statnet's
network package, keeping node, edge, and network attributes:

```{r, eval = has_igraph}
ig <- to_igraph(flo)
igraph::vcount(ig)
head(igraph::vertex_attr(ig, "betweenness"))
karate <- as_netframe(igraph::make_graph("Zachary"))
karate
```

```{r, eval = has_network}
net <- to_network(flo)
network::network.size(net)
```

`to_tbl_graph()` returns a tidygraph object, and the usual generics of
those packages, `igraph::as.igraph()`, `network::as.network()`, and
`tidygraph::as_tbl_graph()`, also accept a netframe.

## Files

`read_network()` and `write_network()` handle GraphML, GEXF, GML, Pajek,
UCINET DL, JSON node-link, ORA's DyNetML, CSV and TSV edge lists, and
(write only) DOT. The format comes from the file extension:

```{r}
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".graphml")
write_network(flo, path)
back <- read_network(path)
back
head(back$nodes)
```

GraphML records attribute types, so the computed columns come back as they
were. An edge list cannot record isolates or node attributes, so a CSV
edge list is written with an optional node file alongside it:

```{r}
edges_csv <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
nodes_csv <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
write_network(flo, edges_csv, nodes_file = nodes_csv)
read_network(edges_csv, nodes = nodes_csv, directed = FALSE)
```
